config.title: Build a tooltip with smart positioning

intro.title: Build a tooltip with smart positioning
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a tooltip component that automatically positions itself around a target element, like a button, to avoid being cut off by the edge of the screen. You'll learn how to use the JavaScript DOM API to calculate the available viewport space and adjust the tooltip's placement dynamically. The core programming concept involves conditionally checking the position of elements and applying different CSS classes based on those calculations. You'll work with event listeners, element measurements, and CSS styling to create a smart, reusable UI feature.
intro.usecase: Smart tooltip positioning is essential in modern web applications where space is limited and user experience is critical. In data dashboards and analytics tools, tooltips dynamically reposition to avoid overlapping with charts, graphs, or other UI elements when displaying detailed metrics. Form builders and design tools use this pattern to show field descriptions or validation hints that adjust based on available screen space. E-commerce platforms implement smart tooltips for product information popups that avoid covering important buttons or images, ensuring smooth shopping experiences.

objectives: Initialize a tooltip component with state to manage visibility
Implement event handlers to control tooltip display on hover
Construct positioning logic to render the tooltip relative to the target element
Apply boundary detection to prevent the tooltip from appearing off-screen
Configure dynamic positioning to switch between top, bottom, left, and right placements
Integrate the tooltip component into a sample user interface
Manipulate CSS properties to style the tooltip and its pointer

steps.title: Import React and useState
steps.instruction: Import React and the useState hook from the 'react' package.
steps.hint: Use the import statement to bring in React and useState from the 'react' module.
steps.analogousExample:
// Importing React and a hook
import React, { useState } from 'react';
steps.expectedOutcome: The React library and useState hook are available for use in the component.
successCriteria: React and useState are imported from 'react'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're importing both React and useState from the 'react' package.
steps.feedbackWrong: That's not quite right. You need to import React and the useState hook from 'react'.

steps.title: Create the main Tooltip component
steps.instruction: Create a functional component named Tooltip that returns null for now.
steps.hint: Define a function called Tooltip that returns null. You can use either a function declaration or an arrow function.
steps.seedCode:
import React, { useState } from 'react';

// Create the Tooltip component here
steps.expectedOutcome: A Tooltip component is defined and returns null.
successCriteria: The Tooltip component is defined and returns null.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you've defined a component named Tooltip that returns null.
steps.feedbackWrong: The Tooltip component isn't defined correctly. Create a function named Tooltip that returns null.

steps.title: Initialize tooltip visibility state
steps.instruction: Inside your Tooltip component, use the useState hook to create a state variable called 'isVisible' and initialize it to false.
steps.hint: Call useState(false) and destructure the returned array into two variables: isVisible and a setter function.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: creating a boolean state variable
const [isActive, setIsActive] = useState(false);
steps.expectedOutcome: The Tooltip component now has an 'isVisible' state variable that tracks whether the tooltip should be shown.
successCriteria: The component contains a useState call that initializes 'isVisible' to false.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using useState with false as the initial value and naming the variable 'isVisible'.
steps.feedbackWrong: Inside the Tooltip component, use useState(false) to create a state variable called 'isVisible'.

steps.title: Create mouse event handlers
steps.instruction: Inside your Tooltip component, create two functions: showTooltip and hideTooltip. The showTooltip function should set isVisible to true, and hideTooltip should set it to false.
steps.hint: Define these functions above the return statement. Use the setter function from useState to update the state.
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have two functions that update the tooltip visibility state when called.
successCriteria: The component contains showTooltip and hideTooltip functions that call setIsVisible with true and false respectively.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure you have both showTooltip and hideTooltip functions, and each should call setIsVisible with the appropriate boolean value.
steps.feedbackWrong: Try creating two separate functions: showTooltip should set isVisible to true, and hideTooltip should set it to false.

steps.title: Add the trigger element structure
steps.instruction: In your Tooltip component's return statement, replace the current `null` with a wrapper `<div>` element that will contain both the trigger button and the tooltip.
steps.hint: Return a JSX `<div>` element instead of `null`. This div will serve as the container for all tooltip elements.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component now returns a `<div>` element that will serve as the container for the tooltip interface.
successCriteria: The Tooltip component returns a JSX `<div>` element instead of `null`.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're returning a `<div>` element from the component.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component should return a `<div>` element to serve as the container for the tooltip interface.

steps.title: Add the trigger button with event wiring
steps.instruction: Inside the component's return statement, add a button element that says 'Hover me' and wire its onMouseEnter and onMouseLeave events to the handlers you will create.
steps.hint: Add a button JSX element with text content and the event handler props. The handlers will be defined in the next step.
steps.expectedOutcome: A button element with 'Hover me' text and placeholder event handler props will be added to the component's structure.
successCriteria: The button element is present with the text 'Hover me' and has onMouseEnter and onMouseLeave props.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You added a button, but check that it includes both onMouseEnter and onMouseLeave props and the text 'Hover me'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The button element is missing or doesn't have the required event handler props. Make sure to add a button with onMouseEnter and onMouseLeave inside the div.

steps.title: Add basic tooltip styling
steps.instruction: Add inline styles to the tooltip div to give it a dark background, white text, padding, rounded corners, and absolute positioning.
steps.hint: Use the style attribute with an object containing CSS properties like backgroundColor, color, padding, borderRadius, and position.
steps.expectedOutcome: The tooltip div now has inline styles that make it visually distinct with a dark background, white text, padding, rounded corners, and absolute positioning.
successCriteria: The tooltip div has a style attribute with at least backgroundColor, color, padding, borderRadius, and position properties.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You added some styling, but make sure to include all the required properties: background color, text color, padding, border radius, and position.
steps.feedbackWrong: The tooltip div doesn't have the expected inline styles. Add a style attribute with properties for background, text color, padding, border radius, and positioning.

steps.title: Initialize tooltip position state
steps.instruction: Inside your Tooltip component, add a new state variable called 'position' and initialize it to the string 'top'.
steps.hint: You'll need to call useState again with the initial value 'top'. Remember to destructure both the state variable and setter function.
steps.expectedOutcome: Your component will now have a 'position' state variable that tracks where the tooltip should appear, starting with 'top' as the default position.
successCriteria: A 'position' state variable is declared using useState and initialized to 'top'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using useState to create a state variable called 'position' with the initial value 'top'.
steps.feedbackWrong: add a new state variable called 'position' initialized to 'top' using the useState hook.

steps.title: Create position calculation function
steps.instruction: Create a function called calculatePosition inside your Tooltip component that takes a trigger element reference and returns an object with 'top' and 'left' CSS values.
steps.hint: The function should calculate where to position the tooltip relative to the trigger element. You can start by returning a simple fixed position for now.
steps.expectedOutcome: A calculatePosition function is defined inside the Tooltip component that returns position coordinates.
successCriteria: The calculatePosition function exists and returns an object with 'top' and 'left' properties.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure the function returns an object with 'top' and 'left' properties.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function should be named calculatePosition and return an object with position coordinates.

steps.title: Integrate positioning into the show handler
steps.instruction: Update the handleMouseEnter function to call calculatePosition and update the position state when the tooltip becomes visible.
steps.hint: Inside handleMouseEnter, after setting isVisible to true, call calculatePosition() and use its return value to update the position state.
steps.expectedOutcome: The handleMouseEnter function will now update both visibility and position states when triggered.
successCriteria: handleMouseEnter calls calculatePosition and updates the position state with its return value.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're both calling calculatePosition and using its return value to update the position state.
steps.feedbackWrong: The handleMouseEnter function needs to do more than just set visibility. It should also calculate and update the position.

steps.title: Apply dynamic positioning to tooltip
steps.instruction: Update the tooltip div's inline style to use the position state values for top and left positioning.
steps.hint: Add a style attribute to the tooltip div that sets top and left CSS properties using the position state values.
steps.analogousExample:
// Similar: applying dynamic positioning
Content
steps.expectedOutcome: The tooltip will appear at the position defined in the position state when visible.
successCriteria: The tooltip div has a style attribute that uses position.top and position.left values for positioning.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure the style attribute uses the position state values for both top and left properties.
steps.feedbackWrong: The tooltip positioning isn't dynamic yet. Add a style attribute to the tooltip div that uses position.top and position.left values.
